The external yolk sac present at the moment of parturition weighs approximately 8.6 grams [Ww0 = approximately 8.6 grams], providing a substantial endogenous nutrient reserve that sustains the neonate during its initial days of independent existence. Hatchlings emerge from their egg cases after an incubation period of 126 days , a duration that aligns closely with values reported for other members of the family Hemiscylliidae maintained at comparable thermal regimes at a temperature of 25 °C [T = 25 °C]. At the time of hatching, these young sharks measure roughly 6*3.54 centimeters  in total length, a measurement that reflects consistent growth within the egg capsule. The weight recorded at this critical transition point averages 14.3 grams , representing a modest increase from the initial yolk mass and signaling the onset of reliance upon exogenous food sources.

As the growing sharks progress through the juvenile and sub-adult phases, their body length increases steadily until they approach the size threshold associated with the onset of gonadal maturation. Field surveys and captive-growth studies indicate that individuals of this species begin transitioning toward reproductive maturity once they attain a total length of approximately 66 centimeters [Lp = approximately 66 centimeters], a benchmark that corresponds to the size at which testicular recrudescence and ovarian maturation are first observed. This length is considerably less than the ultimate total length of 93 centimeters [Li = 93 centimeters] recorded among the largest adults in wild populations, suggesting that a substantial period of somatic growth continues after the initiation of reproductive activity. The corresponding ultimate wet weight recorded among these fully grown individuals reaches as much as 2200 grams [Wwi = 2200 grams], a body mass that places Chiloscyllium plagiosum among the moderate-sized species within its genus. Males and females do not differ markedly in their asymptotic size, although gravid females occasionally attain slightly greater masses due to the combined weight of developing embryos and associated reproductive tissues.

Reproductive output in this species has been characterized under stable captive conditions maintained at 25 °C [T = 25 °C], where females produce eggs at a rate of 22 eggs per 365 days  when they have reached a body length of approximately 83.4 centimeters. This reproductive rate reflects the combined effect of clutch size and inter-clutch interval, with individual females typically depositing one to two fertile egg cases per oviposition event and producing several clutches over the course of a year. The gonadosomatic index (GSI), calculated as the ratio of gonad mass to gonad-free body mass, averaged 2.5% [GSI = 2.5%] in reproductively active individuals at a water temperature of 25 °C [T = 25 °C]. Higher GSI values are generally associated with females approaching the peak of their seasonal breeding cycle, when ovarian follicles are maximally developed and ovulation is imminent.

Longevity records for Chiloscyllium plagiosum maintained in aquaria under stable thermal conditions at 25 °C [T = 25 °C] indicate that the maximum lifespan approaches 25 years [am = 25 years], a duration characteristic of many small-to-medium-sized benthic sharks. This extended survival allows multiple reproductive cycles over the course of an individual's lifetime, with females continuing to produce viable egg cases well into their second decade of life. Physiological senescence, when it does occur, manifests as a gradual decline in reproductive output and a reduction in the frequency of oviposition events rather than a sudden cessation of breeding activity.
